The candidate client is tested against a real loopback HTTP server for: per-request outcomes over all offered requests (status BLOCKED/FAIL/PARTIAL, never COMPLETE); one wall-clock deadline per exchange (0.6s budget, first byte at 0.5s then a stall: 0.604s measured, 1.105s before the fix) that also covers hostname resolution in a disposable child killed and reaped at the deadline (0.4s budget with a stalled lookup: 0.401s measured, 2.008s before; an IP-literal origin starts no child); a cap check before every socket operation with queued-work cancellation; strict finite budget; byte-based token precharge with an operator-declared provider-work bound; canonical origins; fixed error classes with no credential prefix leak; confirmed-only session cleanup; a completed TLS exchange, default certificate verification, a TLS stall, and hostname-not-IP certificate matching and SNI through the resolver are covered with throwaway certificates. The deadline keeps a 0.25s scheduling tolerance and is a client-side guarantee checked against local sockets, not observed behavior of a live target. The independent review's findings are repaired and each is covered by a test that failed first: a gateway tool error is decoded from the parsed result into a fixed enum (capacity and operation_in_progress count as admission rejections, quota and client faults are kept apart, only a not_found answer to a forget of an id this run remembered is a durability error, an unknown code is never reflected); the elapsed preflight counts readiness, per-account setup, the final drain and cleanup (8,535 s for the frozen workload against an 8,100 s schedule); a malformed or deeply nested initialize reply still yields a sanitized receipt and closes the issued session, a close failure cannot discard results, and an integer past 2^63-1 is an invalid budget; a failure measured on dispatched requests is FAIL even when another cap stopped the run, and a run whose shortfall comes only from never-dispatched arrivals stays BLOCKED; the fact vocabulary keeps the frozen 32 to 512 word range under the gateway's 4,096-byte limit (at most 4,095 bytes, no truncation). Word counts are nominal, not provider-billed tokens. limitations: No supported live-load execution: CLI is fail-closed until live-enable-requirements.md is satisfied. The candidate client has loopback-server tests only and never reports better than PARTIAL.

The per-exchange deadline covers hostname resolution (a disposable child, killed and reaped at the deadline), connect, TLS, headers and body under one monotonic deadline, within a 0.25s scheduling tolerance plus child start and post-deadline SIGTERM/SIGKILL/reap time (up to 1.2s if a child survives SIGTERM and SIGKILL). It runs the host's operating-system resolver unmodified, tries addresses sequentially, and adds one child (20-37ms measured locally) to each hostname exchange's recorded latency. It is checked against local sockets and a scripted resolver only; it says nothing about a live target or DNS provider.

Token precharge is encoded argument bytes (an upper bound, no tokenizer verified), plus an operator-declared provider_work_bound for server-side work the client cannot observe. The committed manifest leaves that bound null, so a live run stays blocked.

No provider calls or deployment occurred. No complete cost or capacity qualification is claimed. Deadline and resolver tests are timing-based against real sockets and child processes and could flake on a heavily loaded host.

EC2 regional pricing parity, backup byte sizes, mixes, query/rebuild/readiness usage and shared-account free allowances remain assumptions; provider price, log volumes, custom metrics and restore activity remain unknown.
Backup lifecycle model assumes about 60 days of full timestamped snapshots and needs measured/architecture validation; its full-limit exposure exceeds the historical $60 ceiling.

Workload word counts are nominal sizes of synthetic text, not gateway-metered or provider-billed tokens; no tokenizer is assumed. The gateway meters with its own tokenizer, so real token use per request can differ from the nominal figure.

The frozen hot tenant offers the gateway's 120 requests-per-minute account limit. The simulator's limiter reproduces the gateway's fixed window that starts at an account's first request and the 600 per minute address limit, but counts offered arrivals only, so live counts can differ by a few requests per window from setup and cleanup requests. Rejections are counted as failures, not excluded.

Every request sends Connection: close and pays a fresh TCP and TLS handshake, and latency runs from dispatch, not from the scheduled arrival, so client-side queueing behind the eight workers is not in the recorded p95. Read latency and handshake-load figures with both in mind.
